content: 1. Treatment of multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB) meningitis (TBM) in children and adolescents should prioritize medications with good cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) penetration. These include fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin), linezolid, cycloserine/terizidone, and ethionamide (if susceptibility is likely). 2. Regimens for MDR/RR-TB meningitis should ideally include at least three drugs with good CSF penetration. Additional medications should be added based on disease severity and treatment principles. 3. For pulmonary disease coexisting with central nervous system (CNS) disease, the addition of bedaquiline should be considered. 4. Linezolid may need to be used for longer durations in MDR/RR-TB meningitis, potentially throughout the treatment course, due to its excellent CSF penetration and limited alternative options, provided it is well-tolerated. 5. Most other forms of extrapulmonary MDR/RR-TB can be treated similarly to pulmonary MDR/RR-TB using longer regimens. 6. Osteoarticular MDR/RR-TB, including spinal TB, typically requires treatment for at least 18 months due to concerns about bone penetration of TB drugs and the severity of the disease. 7. The most clinically significant drug-drug interaction with antiretroviral therapy (ART) involves bedaquiline. ART regimens containing integrase inhibitors like dolutegravir (DTG) are preferred for children with HIV receiving bedaquiline, as significant interactions are not expected. 8. ART regimens containing efavirenz (EFV) should be avoided in children and adolescents on bedaquiline, as EFV significantly reduces bedaquiline concentrations. 9. Co-treatment with lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) may increase bedaquiline exposure but has not been associated with increased adverse effects, so it can be considered with careful monitoring. 10. Nevirapine (NVP)-containing regimens are not ideal due to reduced efficacy, and substitution with EFV is not an option. 11. Triple nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) regimens are not routinely recommended, especially in cases of high viral load, due to reduced potency. 12. TB medications should generally be dosed according to body weight. Monthly weight monitoring is crucial in children and adolescents, with dose adjustments as they gain weight. 13. The bioavailability of bedaquiline, delamanid, and clofazimine is significantly improved when taken with food, particularly high-fat meals, and should be administered with food whenever possible. 14. Delamanid should ideally be administered separately from other medications by at least one hour to avoid potential negative effects on its absorption. 15. Child-friendly dispersible formulations of many second-line TB drugs have been developed and are preferred for treating young children with MDR/RR-TB. These formulations are easier to administer and avoid the need to manipulate adult formulations. 16. If child-friendly formulations are unavailable, manipulated adult formulations (e.g., crushed or dissolved tablets) can be used, provided bioequivalence data exist. 17. Bedaquiline adult tablets (100 mg) crushed and suspended in water have been shown to be bioequivalent to whole tablets and can be used in children if dispersible formulations are unavailable. 18. Extemporaneous liquid formulations of bedaquiline and delamanid can be prepared using adult tablets, with sugar-containing and sugar-free options available. 19. Monitoring children and adolescents on MDR/RR-TB treatment involves regular clinical, radiological, and microbiological assessments to evaluate treatment response, detect treatment failure early, and monitor for adverse events. 20. Clinical improvement and weight gain are the best indicators of a positive response to treatment. Regular weight monitoring and nutritional assessments are essential. 21. Radiographic abnormalities from TB may resolve slowly, and some may persist until the end of treatment. Worsening symptoms, failure to gain weight, or weight loss may indicate treatment failure and require further assessment. 22. Patients receiving QT-prolonging medications (e.g., clofazimine, bedaquiline, delamanid, fluoroquinolones) should undergo regular electrocardiogram (ECG) monitoring. Baseline, 2-week, 4-week, and then monthly ECGs are recommended, with additional monitoring as clinically indicated. 23. QTc prolongation over 450 ms is considered prolonged, and QTc ≥500 ms significantly increases the risk of life-threatening arrhythmias. In such cases, withholding or adjusting QT-prolonging medications should be considered. 24. Linezolid is associated with bone marrow toxicity, including anemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia, which are doseand duration-dependent. Regular full blood count monitoring is essential, especially during prolonged treatment.
